articles.title: Socially isolated and lonely people tend to be biologically older than their years
articles.summary: Having no one to confide in was linked to an older biological age about as strongly as feeling lonely, according to a study of more than 300,000 adults that also tied isolation and loneliness to higher mortality.

articles.title: Brain structure carries clues about who prefers instant gratification, study suggests
articles.summary: Would you take $20 today or $50 next month? A new brain imaging study suggests the answer may be partly reflected in the volumes of brain regions tied to reward and long-term planning.

articles.title: House Republicans accuse the American Psychological Association of tolerating antisemitism
articles.summary: A House Republican report accuses the American Psychological Association of letting antisemitism fester and dismissing Jewish psychologists’ concerns, citing internal emails. The APA rejects the findings and says it unequivocally condemns antisemitism.

articles.title: Can watching sports make voters accept political defeats?
articles.summary: Watching athletes and coaches gracefully accept defeat in televised sports can make voters more accepting of political losses. New research shows that observing good sportsmanship directly increases the likelihood that voters will believe an unfavorable election was fair.

articles.title: Curriculum unlearning in humans and neural networks
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.04565v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: During learning, humans often benefit from curricula that teach simple rules before exceptions. However, we lack a computational explanation for this phenomenon. Here, using a canonical behavioural task and modelling with neural networks, we develop and test a theory for why simple-to-complex curricula succeed. We show that during learning, both humans and neural networks show simplicity biases, a tendency to learn simple rules that are underfit to the data. In neural networks this bias is accompanied by compression of neural representations. S

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work

articles.title: Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that a drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries can tackle several key features of Alzheimer’s disease, including DNA damage and inflammation. Already tested for initial safety in humans, the experimental treatment could offer a faster path toward therapies that target the disease at its roots.

articles.title: New research reveals the psychological profile of reality dating television stars
articles.summary: People who volunteer for reality dating shows display higher levels of grandiose narcissism and a stronger reliance on physical appearance for their self-esteem, according to new research. The study explores the specific personality traits driving televised romance.

articles.summary: Can when you eat affect your brain? In a small study, men with metabolic syndrome who ate only between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. for a month showed memory gains and gray matter increases in memory-related regions.

articles.title: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired
articles.summary: Scientists propose that the brain’s mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.

articles.title: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success
articles.summary: A massive new study reveals that intelligence plays a surprisingly limited role in children's reading success, while visual processing showed no meaningful connection at all. Instead, the strongest predictors are sound recognition, vocabulary, and background knowledge, offering new clues about how to help struggling readers.

articles.title: The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
articles.summary: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely safe situations.

articles.title: Alignment Faking Depends on the Value, Not Just the Model
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.03650v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models can follow a directive when they believe they are monitored and abandon it when they believe they are not, a pattern termed Alignment Faking. Prior work establishes this for harmful-content objectives and a handful of moral-foundations values, leaving open how it distributes across a wider value space. We argue it is value-dependent: whether compliance survives a change in perceived oversight is a property of the model--value pairing, not of the model alone. Our framework profiles Alignment Faking per value, scoring each model-val

articles.title: CARD: A Proof-Carrying Certificate-to-Action Interface for Relative-Measurement Graphs
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.03651v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Geometric certificates make mathematical claims about specified estimator objects, while robotic action requires a physical transform, a service decision, and timely proof support. We present CARD, a proof-carrying interface that keeps these objects distinct and records how they combine. Its lifted-fiber formulation separates semantic motion from witness repair and characterizes when projected and proof-carrying costs coincide. Its actionability result gives an exact useful-service law: uniform sampling without replacement produces a hypergeometr
